extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of short satirical/moral character essays (readers of The Spectator); educated 18th-century literate public
extracted.subtask_description: Short satirical/moral essays that sketch eccentric country characters and use anecdote, visual detail, and learned asides to amuse and instruct. Emphasis on novelty of character, concrete specifics, and a blend of humour with moral reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek odd and uncommon characters / novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Odd and uncommon Characters are the Game that I look for, and most delight in; for which Reason I was as much pleased with the Novelty of the Person that talked to me..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer featuring unusual, eccentric, or novel personalities — these provide the primary amusement and hold reader attention. The narrator explicitly values novelty as the source of delight; anecdotes about striking small events (catching a huge jack, springing a pheasant) are used to foreground the character's peculiarity and entertain the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define characters by small, tangible, quirky details
rubrics_metrics.description: Character shown through concrete little handicrafts and habits: "He makes a May-fly to a Miracle; and furnishes the whole Country with Angle-Rods... carries a Tulip-root in his Pocket... presents a Pair of Garters of his own knitting... raises a great deal of Mirth ... by enquiring as often as he meets them 'how they wear'?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific, odd possessions, hobbies, and small repeated behaviours to render a character vivid and endearing (or ridiculous). Such minutiae make a sketch memorable and can produce comic effect by contrast with the character's social station.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lively anecdotes and scene details to animate the narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Long, vivid accounts of actions (hooking and playing a huge fish, describing how he sprung a pheasant, the dining scene with the fish served) furnish the conversation and entertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell short dramatic incidents with sensory and sequential detail rather than abstract summary. Set scenes (dinner, walks, galleries) and play out the action to produce humour and keep the reader engaged. Recounting the mechanics of an exploit (how the fish was hooked and drawn out) is a comic device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend humour with moral and social reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: After humorous description the narrator reflects: "I was secretly touched with Compassion ... how so good a Heart and such busy Hands were wholly employed in Trifles ... What Good to his Country or himself might not a Trader or Merchant have done with such useful tho' ordinary qualifications?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair entertaining sketches with a moral or social observation — e.g., the waste of talent, pride of gentility, or national advantages of trade — so the piece amuses but also instructs. Use the character as a springboard for broader commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a colloquial, blunt character voice and conversational narration
rubrics_metrics.description: "He entered into the Matter, after his blunt way of saying Things, as they occur to his Imagination, without regular Introduction, or Care to preserve the Appearance of Chain of Thought."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let characters speak in a natural, sometimes disordered fashion to preserve realism and comic effect. A speaker's bluntness, local idiom, and offhand remarks can reveal social values and produce humour; the narrator can adopt a similarly amiable, observant tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit observational comparisons (dress, manners, generations) for comic insight
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is worth while to consider the Force of Dress; and how the Persons of one Age differ from those of another, merely by that only. One may observe also, that the general Fashion of one Age has been followed by one particular Set of People in another..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts across time, class, or fashion (dress, posture, accessories) to make satirical or humorous points about pretension, preservation of habit, or absurdity. Visual comparison is a source of wit and social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical juxtaposition and ironic praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions that pair opposite qualities for ironic effect: e.g., Sir Humphrey was "in his Dealings as punctual as a Tradesman, and as generous as a Gentleman"; another ancestor "left the Estate with ten thousand Pounds Debt upon it, but ... was every way the finest Gentleman in the World."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use irony and juxtaposition — praising a vice or buffoonery in elevated terms — to satirise social types. Let laudatory language highlight the absurdity of behaviour or values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete visual devices (galleries, portraits, objects) to tell family/history and reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: The gallery and portraits are used as prompts for stories about ancestors, dress, and deeds: broken lances, viols, petticoats, library receipts for recipes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame narrative around visual prompts (pictures, objects, rooms) to allow retrospection, anecdote, and comic historical sketches. Objects anchor stories and supply comic or moral contrasts between past and present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support reflections with learned references and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay invokes Locke, Lucretius, Josephus and classical lines in discussing ghosts, association of ideas, and the immortality of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bolster amusing or speculative reflections by briefly invoking philosophers, classical poets, or historians — this adds erudition, variety of tone, and a didactic weight to the comic essay. Use citations sparingly to lend credibility or to set up an ironic contrast between learning and common superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclude anecdotes with a moral or general maxim
rubrics_metrics.description: After telling ghostly anecdotes and a story from Josephus the author closes: "If any Man thinks these Facts incredible, let him enjoy his own Opinion to himself, but let him not endeavour to disturb the Belief of others, who by Instances of this Nature are excited to the Study of Virtue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: End sketches by extracting a moral, lesson, or universal observation that connects the particular comic instance to broader human concerns (virtue, charity, belief). This turns entertainment into instruction and anchors the essay's purpose.
